title: Caching
subtitle: Keep the hot answers close — and pay for the second copy
objectives: Explain why caching works at all — and why it's a bet on skewed traffic, not on cache size
Wire a cache correctly: cache-aside, the write patterns, and local vs shared
Reason about eviction, and read the miss rate rather than the hit rate
Diagnose the hard parts: invalidation, stampedes, the stale-set race, and a cache that's quietly load-bearing

exercises.prompt: Your product page runs the same expensive database query 10,000 times a second. Every single run returns an identical result. What's the cheapest fix?
choices: Buy a faster database
Run the query once, keep the answer somewhere fast, and hand out that copy
Add more application servers
Ask users to refresh less often
exercises.why: Nothing about that query got cheaper — you just stopped running it 9,999 times. That's the whole idea: the fastest work is work you skip. Notice the other options scale the waste instead of removing it — a faster database runs the same pointless query faster, and more app servers generate more copies of it. And caching only pays off because the answer gets reused: if all 10,000 requests wanted different results, there'd be nothing to hand out.

exercises.prompt: A ______ stores the result of expensive work so the next request gets the answer without redoing it.
choices: cache
queue
replica
index
exercises.why: Store the answer, skip the work. It's worth seeing what a cache is NOT, since the other three are real things you'll meet: a replica (unit 10) is a full copy kept deliberately in sync, and an index (unit 8) makes the work itself cheaper. A cache does neither. It just remembers a result it happened to see, and it's allowed to forget it at any moment.

exercises.prompt: Your database holds 50 million products. Your cache holds 50,000 — one thousandth of them. Why isn't that hopeless?
choices: Because the cache is faster, so it makes up the difference
Because requests aren't spread evenly — a small set of products gets asked for constantly, and that set fits
Because the cache compresses the data
Because 50,000 is enough for most databases
exercises.why: Real traffic is wildly lopsided: a handful of products — the front page, the viral one, today's deal — absorb a huge share of requests, and that hot set is small enough to fit. Caching is a bet on that skew, which means whether it works is a property of your TRAFFIC, not your cache. Flip it around to feel it: if all 50 million products were requested uniformly at random, a 50,000-item cache would hit about 0.1% of the time, and you'd have added a network hop, a config, and a staleness bug for nothing.

exercises.prompt: Match each read to roughly what it costs (order-of-magnitude, not precise).

pairs.left: Cache over the network, same datacenter

exercises.why: The jump that surprises people is the second one. A Redis lookup isn't fast because memory is fast — it's roughly 5,000× slower than the memory in your own process, because you're paying a network round trip (unit 4) and barely touching the memory at all. It only looks fast next to the thing it replaced. That gap is exactly why an in-process cache and a shared cache are two different tools rather than the same tool in two sizes.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are good things to cache? Select all.
choices: A product page that changes twice a year and is viewed a million times a day
A slow report that every user on the dashboard requests
A user's current account balance, read to decide whether a transfer clears
A 'trending now' feed that's expensive to compute and fine a minute out of date
exercises.why: The pattern is three conditions at once: expensive to produce, read far more than written, and tolerant of being slightly stale. The balance fails the third — and it fails for the reader's sake rather than because it changes often; unit 5 already settled that a balance is the one number the user came to see. But cacheability really is a property of the READ rather than of the data, and stock count shows it cleanly: '12 left' on a browse page can be a minute stale and nobody is harmed, while the same number checked at checkout must be exact or you've just oversold the item.

exercises.prompt: You add a cache. What have you unavoidably introduced?
choices: A second copy of the data that is allowed to disagree with the source of truth
A slower system
A new database
Nothing — it's a pure win
exercises.why: A cache is a copy, so unit 5's rule applies the moment you add one: truth now lives in two places, they can disagree, and you own the question of how wrong you'll let the copy get. Every hard part of this unit — invalidation, TTLs, the races in lesson 4 — is the bill for that one sentence. Caching gets pitched as free speed. It isn't: you bought latency with correctness, and the only question left is how much correctness you're spending.

exercises.prompt: Order a cache-aside read — the most common wiring.
steps: App asks the cache for key 'product:42'
Cache misses — it doesn't have it
App writes the result into the cache
App returns the result to the user
exercises.why: The app orchestrates every step here, which is exactly what 'aside' means: in this pattern the cache is a dumb box that stores what it's told and never talks to the database itself. That buys a property worth noticing — if the cache is empty or dead, this path still works, it's just slow. Being able to degrade to 'merely slow' rather than 'broken' is a large part of why cache-aside dominates in practice.

exercises.prompt: Cache-aside is also called ______ loading, because an item only enters the cache when someone actually asks for it.
choices: lazy
eager
write
bulk
exercises.why: Populate on demand. The upside is that you never spend memory on data nobody has asked for, so real traffic shapes the cache's contents with no guesswork from you — though note that's a weaker promise than it sounds, since anything that was popular once keeps its slot until eviction gets around to it. The downside is the mirror image of the upside: every item's first request is guaranteed to miss, so a freshly-started cache misses everything at once, which is why 'just restart the cache' is a sentence that has taken down real sites.

exercises.prompt: Match each caching pattern to how it works.

pairs.right: App checks the cache, and on a miss loads from the DB itself
App only talks to the cache; the cache loads from the DB on a miss
Writes go to cache and DB together, before the write is acknowledged
Writes land in the cache and flush to the DB later

exercises.why: The two read patterns differ only in who does the fetching on a miss — the app or the cache — which is a question about where complexity lives, not about what the user experiences. The write patterns are the ones with teeth: write-through pays latency on every single write to keep the cache warm and avoid a first-read miss, while write-behind makes writes feel instant by acknowledging data that isn't durable yet. Note what write-through does NOT buy — correctness under concurrency. It's still update-on-write, so two writers can land in the cache in the opposite order they landed in the database, exactly as lesson 4 shows.

exercises.prompt: Write-behind acknowledges a write as soon as it's in the cache, then flushes to the database a moment later. What did you just trade away?
choices: Read speed
Durability — you told the user 'saved' while the only copy sat in memory that can vanish
The ability to cache reads
Nothing — the flush always succeeds eventually
exercises.why: You moved the acknowledgement earlier than the persistence, and everything in that window is a promise you can't keep. If the cache node dies before the flush, the data is gone AND the user was told it was saved — the worst pairing available, because nobody retries something they believe succeeded. This is unit 9's D in ACID, handed over deliberately in exchange for speed. Defensible for view counts and metrics; indefensible for an order.

exercises.prompt: Place the missing piece: the app should check for a saved answer before doing the expensive database work.
exercises.why: A cache goes on the read path, in front of whatever you want to do less of — that's the general shape, and it's why you'll see caches at every layer of a real system rather than at one 'correct' spot. The position is what makes it useful and dangerous at the same time: reads now consult a component that is explicitly allowed to be out of date.

exercises.prompt: You use cache-aside at a 95% hit rate. Your Redis cluster dies completely, at peak traffic. What happens?
choices: Every request goes straight to the database — which suddenly takes 20× its normal read load and may fall over
The app crashes
Writes fail
Nothing changes
exercises.why: The code degrades correctly — a miss just means 'ask the database' — so nothing is logically broken. The trap is capacity. At a 95% hit rate your database was quietly serving 5% of reads, so losing the cache multiplies its load by twenty in an instant, and unless someone deliberately sized it for the uncached load, twenty times is not a margin much survives. The cache wasn't an optimization, it was load-bearing, and the database has no idea it was being protected. This is why 'the cache is just a speedup' is a dangerous thing to believe.

exercises.prompt: You cache in each app server's own memory instead of a shared Redis. What's the catch?
choices: It's slower than a shared cache
Each server has its own copy — so they can disagree with each other, and every server must warm up separately
It can't store structured objects
There's no catch
exercises.why: In-process caching is genuinely appealing: roughly 5,000× faster per hit by lesson 1's ladder, with no network hop to fail. What you pay is consistency and warmth. N servers means N copies means N versions of the truth, so a user hitting refresh can bounce between two different answers depending on where the load balancer (unit 12) sends them. You also multiply memory by N, and every deploy throws all of it away at once. A shared cache trades a network hop for one answer everybody agrees on.

lessons.title: Eviction & the hit rate that matters

exercises.prompt: Your cache's memory fills up. A new item needs to go in. What has to happen?
choices: Something already in the cache gets thrown out to make room
The cache grows itself to fit
The item is stored on disk instead
The oldest item moves back to the database
exercises.why: A cache is finite on purpose — something that held everything wouldn't be a cache, it'd be a copy of your database with no durability guarantee. So it lives in a permanent state of deciding what to forget, and that decision is the entire game: identical hardware can give you a 60% hit rate or a 95% one depending purely on what it chooses to throw away.

exercises.prompt: Match each eviction policy to what it throws out.

pairs.right: Whatever hasn't been touched for the longest
Whatever gets asked for least often
Anything past its expiry, popular or not

exercises.why: `LRU` is the default nearly everywhere because recency is a cheap and decent predictor of the near future. LFU beats it when popularity is stable, but it clings to items that were huge last month and are dead now, unless you age the counts. `TTL` is the odd one out and it's worth seeing why: `LRU` throws things out because you ran out of room, `TTL` throws them out because you stopped trusting them — space versus correctness, two different problems wearing the same clothes. Random sounds like a joke and isn't: it needs no bookkeeping and performs respectably.

exercises.prompt: Your `LRU` cache holds the 50,000 hottest products at a 96% hit rate. A nightly job starts reading all 50 million products once, in order. What happens?
choices: Nothing — the job's reads get cached too
The hit rate collapses: every scanned item counts as 'recently used', so the scan evicts the entire hot set for data nobody will ask for again
It improves — more data is now cached
The cache rejects the job's reads
exercises.why: `LRU` assumes recently-used predicts soon-to-be-used, and a sequential scan violates that assumption perfectly: every item it touches is maximally recent and minimally likely to be needed again. So the scan flushes your hot set, users start hitting the database, and the cache sits there full of garbage. That's cache pollution, and it's why a batch job can take down a site it never queries — the damage is entirely collateral. The fixes are to keep scans off the cache path, or to use a policy that makes an item earn its place with a second access.

exercises.prompt: A cache hit takes 1ms. A miss costs 100ms all-in. At a 95% hit rate, what's the average read latency in milliseconds?
exercises.why: 0.95 × 1ms + 0.05 × 100ms = 5.95ms. Now look at where that number came from: the 5% that miss contribute 5ms of the 5.95, so about 84% of your average latency is produced by one request in twenty. That's the shape of every cache — the misses own the average and the hits are nearly irrelevant to it, which is why tuning the hit path is almost always the wrong place to spend your afternoon.

exercises.prompt: Your hit rate is 90%. You tune it to 99%. That's only 9 points. Why is it actually enormous?
choices: It isn't — 9% is marginal
Because the misses are what cost you: 10% → 1% is one tenth as many misses, so one tenth the database load
Because the cache got faster
Because 99% is a round number
exercises.why: Always read the miss rate, not the hit rate — 'hit rate' is a vanity framing that squashes the entire interesting range into a sliver at the top. Said properly, 90 → 99 removed 90% of your remaining misses, so your database's read load dropped 10×. In this lesson's numbers the average read falls from 10.9ms to 1.99ms. And the logic keeps going: 99% → 99.9% is another 10× cut, which is exactly why teams up here fight over fractions of a percent that sound absurd from the outside.

exercises.prompt: Which of these actually raise your hit RATE? Select all.
choices: More cache memory, so the hot set fits
A longer `TTL`, so entries live long enough to be reused
Keeping batch scans off the cache so they can't evict the hot set
A faster network to the cache
exercises.why: Three things decide hit rate: whether the hot set fits, whether entries survive long enough to be reused, and whether anything is polluting the cache. A faster network makes each hit cheaper — that's hit LATENCY, a different axis entirely, and it does nothing to the rate. Keep them separate, because 'the cache is slow' and 'the cache is missing' have opposite fixes and the second is nearly always the bigger number. Note the second option isn't free either: every extra second of `TTL` is another second you've agreed to be wrong.

exercises.prompt: You set a 60-second `TTL` on a cached value. What have you actually decided?
choices: That the value takes 60 seconds to compute
That you're willing to serve data up to 60 seconds out of date
That the value will be refreshed every 60 seconds
That the cache holds 60 seconds of data
exercises.why: A `TTL` is a correctness decision wearing a performance costume: you're stating the maximum lag you'll tolerate between the source of truth and what users see. That's what makes it the pragmatic escape from invalidation (lesson 4) — rather than tracking every change perfectly, you promise to be wrong for at most 60 seconds. And it's a ceiling, not a schedule: with lazy loading nothing refreshes on a timer, the entry simply expires, and the next reader — whenever they show up, in a second or an hour — pays to rebuild it.

exercises.prompt: Phil Karlton's famous line: 'There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.' Why is invalidation genuinely hard?
choices: Deleting a key is computationally expensive
Knowing WHICH keys a change affects — and finding all of them — is the hard part, and getting it wrong is silent
Caches don't support deletion
It requires taking the cache offline
exercises.why: Deleting a key is trivial; the hard part is the question that comes before it. One product's price changing might invalidate the product page, three category listings, a search result, and a homepage module — and nothing in your system tells you that. What makes it vicious is the failure mode: a missed invalidation throws no error and appears in no log. It just serves a wrong answer, confidently, until something else happens to evict it. Bugs that page you are easy. Bugs that quietly lie for a week are hard.

exercises.prompt: On a write, should you update the cached value or just delete it?
choices: Update it — that keeps the cache warm
Usually delete it: updating computes a value nobody asked for, and races with other writers over whose version lands last
Neither — let the `TTL` handle it
Both, for safety
exercises.why: Deleting is safe precisely because it isn't a claim about anything — it says 'I don't know', and the next reader rebuilds from the source of truth. Updating asserts a value, so two concurrent writers can land their updates in the cache in the opposite order they landed them in the database, leaving the cache permanently disagreeing with the DB and no error raised anywhere. You also pay to compute a value that may never be read. Delete is the humbler operation, and humility buys a lot here.

exercises.prompt: One extremely popular key — your homepage feed, 10,000 requests/sec — hits its `TTL` and expires. What happens in the next instant?
choices: The cache rebuilds it automatically before anyone notices
All 10,000 requests miss at once, and every one of them runs the expensive rebuild against the database simultaneously
One request rebuilds it and the rest wait
The requests queue up behind the first one
exercises.why: Nothing coordinates them. Each request independently checks the cache, sees nothing, and does exactly what it was told: go rebuild it. So a query your database saw zero times per second now arrives 10,000 times in the same instant — and the more popular the key, the harder the hit, which means your best-cached content is your biggest liability. This is a cache stampede (or thundering herd), and it's a favourite way for a site to die at a moment when nothing was wrong: no traffic spike, no deploy, no failure. Just a timer expiring.

exercises.prompt: Which of these actually help against a cache stampede? Select all.
choices: A lock, so only the first request rebuilds and the others wait for it
Serve the stale value while one request refreshes it in the background
Add jitter to TTLs so a batch of keys doesn't all expire in the same instant
Shorten the `TTL` so it happens more often but costs less each time
exercises.why: The first two attack the herd directly: let exactly one request through, and either make the rest wait or hand them slightly-stale data — usually the nicer option, since nobody experiences a stall at all. Jitter attacks a related killer, where keys cached together (everything warmed at deploy, say) expire together, turning one expiry into a synchronized fleet-wide miss. Shortening the `TTL` makes both problems worse: more stampedes, and no reduction in the size of any one herd. Facebook's memcache team hit this hard enough at scale to invent leases for it, described in their 2013 paper.

exercises.prompt: Two things happen at once. Request A misses and reads value V1 from the database. Before A writes it back, request B writes V2 to the database and deletes the cache key — which is already empty, so that's a no-op. Then A writes V1 into the cache. What's the state?
choices: The cache holds V2 — correct
The cache holds V1 while the database holds V2, and the invalidation already happened, so nothing will fix it until the `TTL` expires
The cache is empty
A's write fails
exercises.why: Neither request did anything wrong. A read a value that was true when it read it and wrote it back a moment later; B wrote and dutifully invalidated. But B's invalidation landed in the gap between A's read and A's write, so it deleted nothing, and then A resurrected a dead value on top of it. The cache is now confidently wrong and no future event will correct it — only the `TTL` will, which is why even a perfectly-invalidated cache still needs one as a backstop. This is the race Facebook's leases exist to close: A takes a lease on the miss, B's write voids it, and A's stale set gets rejected. Take the general lesson too — a cache plus a database is two copies with no coordination between them, so you're doing distributed systems now whether you signed up for it or not.

exercises.prompt: You're picking a `TTL` for a product's price, shown on a page viewed a million times a day. Slide toward your choice.
exercises.why: Prices are the classic case where staleness has a bill attached — show $8, charge $10, and you have a support problem and possibly a legal one — so this leans short. But the question is a little bit of a trap: `TTL` is your worst tool here. A price change is an EVENT you already know about, so invalidate on the write and the cache is correct within milliseconds no matter what the `TTL` says, which frees the `TTL` to do what it's genuinely good at — backstopping the invalidations you'll inevitably miss, including the race in the previous exercise. Reach for a very long `TTL` only when you're confident invalidation is airtight, and a very short one only when you can't detect the change at all and you're reduced to polling.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of caching?
choices: It makes your system fast for free
It buys latency and backend relief by keeping a second copy that's allowed to be wrong — and hands you invalidation, eviction, stampedes, and a component your system now secretly depends on
It's only needed above millions of users
It removes the need for a fast database
exercises.why: Caching is the highest-leverage move in this tier — a 95% hit rate takes 20× the read load off your database for the price of some memory — and it's sold as free speed, which is the lie. Look at what you actually took on: a second copy of the truth (unit 5), a race you can't reliably test your way out of, a component whose loss multiplies your database load 20× at the worst possible moment, and a class of bug that never raises an error. Cache when the read is expensive, reused, and tolerant of being stale — and when you do, decide out loud how wrong you'll let it be, because a `TTL` you didn't think about is still an answer to that question.
